Fitted Value Methods

The previous chapter studied function iteration with a known model: when a fit preserves the contraction of the Bellman operator, and how far the iteration ends from v∗v^*v∗ when each fit is accurate. This chapter turns that iteration into a learning algorithm. Three things change. The fit becomes any regressor, a tree ensemble or a neural network, which turns function iteration into fitted value iteration, a sequence of regression problems whose targets are Bellman backups. The expectations in those targets become averages over sampled successors, because a simulator or a log of transitions is often all there is. And the values of states become values of actions, so that acting needs no model. Run on a fixed log of transitions, the result is fitted Q-iteration, the batch algorithm behind tree-based FQI and NFQ, and the starting point of DQN in the next chapter. Replacing exact expectations by samples is what turns approximate dynamic programming into what the operations research community calls simulation-based dynamic programming and the machine learning community calls reinforcement learning.

Sampling has two costs that the chapter makes explicit. The error of a sample average is random rather than systematic; its rate does not depend on the dimension of the state, and it adds to the per-iteration error that the previous chapter bounded. And the maximum over noisy estimates is biased upward, even though each estimate is unbiased, so the targets of every sampled Bellman update overestimate. Between the two, temporal-difference learning solves the Galerkin system of the previous chapter one transition at a time, and shows how sampling with the wrong weighting can make a well-posed equation diverge. The chapter ends with fitted Q-iteration on two logs, one from an inference-serving scheduler and one of the collision warnings that ESA received for its satellites.

Learning Goals

After completing this chapter, you should be able to:

  • Write fitted value iteration for an arbitrary regressor, and recognize collocation and Galerkin projection as two choices of the fitting rule

  • Bound the error of fitted value iteration, and the loss of its greedy policy, by the error of each fit

  • Locate the two expectations in a fitted Bellman update, inside the operator and over the states, and bound the effect of estimating either one on the fixed point

  • Replace an expectation by a sample average, state the bias and variance of the result, and explain why its rate is independent of the dimension

  • Define the action-value function and its Bellman operator, and explain what it saves at decision time

  • Derive TD(0) as a stochastic solver of the Galerkin system, and explain why it is stable on-policy and can diverge off-policy

  • Derive the upward bias of a maximum over noisy estimates, and explain how decoupling selection from evaluation removes part of it

  • Write fitted Q-iteration on a fixed set of transitions, and attribute the errors of a fitted policy to approximation, where actions are nearly tied, or to coverage, where the data never tried an action

Prerequisites: the convergence results for approximate value iteration (previous chapter), the weighted-residual template (parametric value functions), basic probability (expectation, variance, the central limit theorem, Jensen’s inequality).

Fitted Value Iteration with an Arbitrary Regressor¶

The averager condition is a property of how a fit maps targets to a function, not of a basis: kernel smoothers and fixed-partition trees satisfy it without one. The error bound of Error Bounds When Every Fit Is Accurate below needs even less, only that each fit be accurate. Nothing ties function iteration to a basis, then, and the fit can be any regression procedure, including the tree ensembles and neural networks of the chapters ahead.

Value iteration computes Lvk\Bellman v_kLvk​ at every state and stores the result. With a parametric function we can do neither, but we can do two things that together play the same role. We can evaluate the Bellman operator at finitely many states s1,…,sms_1, \ldots, s_ms1​,…,sm​,

Write P\ProjP for the map that takes a function, through its values at s1,…,sms_1, \ldots, s_ms1​,…,sm​, to the fitted function. Then fitted value iteration is

vk+1=PLvk,v_{k+1} = \Proj \Bellman v_k,vk+1​=PLvk​,
(2)

the projected value iteration (25) of the chapter on parametric value functions, with P\ProjP now any fitting rule. Two choices define the algorithm: where the targets are computed, and how the function is fitted to them. Nothing depends on the max. Replacing L\BellmanL by the policy evaluation operator Lπ\BellmanPiLπ​ gives fitted policy evaluation, and replacing it by the smooth operator Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ of Regularized Bellman Operators gives fitted smooth value iteration.

The algorithm is two nested loops. The outer loop is successive approximation: it computes Bellman targets from the current function and holds them fixed. The inner loop is an optimization: it fits the function to those targets, in closed form for a linear basis, by building trees for a tree ensemble, or by gradient steps for a neural network. We call every algorithm with this structure a fitted value method. Gordon (1995) gave the first analysis of when it converges. The fitted Q-iteration of Ernst et al. (2005) is one instance, with extremely randomized trees as the fit and action values in place of state values; NFQ Riedmiller (2005) is another, with a neural network. The algorithms of the coming chapters differ mainly in how far the inner loop is run before the targets are recomputed.

The two fits of the chapter on parametric value functions mark the ends of a range. Collocation computes targets at exactly nnn states, as many as there are basis functions, and interpolates them: P\ProjP is the interpolation operator, and with piecewise-linear cardinal functions on a grid the algorithm is the stationary version of the interpolated backward recursion (16) of the finite-horizon chapter. Galerkin projection computes targets at as many states as the quadrature needs and fits the basis to them by weighted least squares: P\ProjP is the www-orthogonal projection onto the span of the basis, and when the states are sampled from www the fit is an ordinary regression. Collocation computes few targets and matches them exactly; regression computes many and matches them on average. Regression is what scales, because it decouples the number of targets from the number of parameters, and because it applies unchanged to any model that can be fitted to data.

Fitting a Neural Network: Fixed Targets and the Semi-Gradient¶

For a model v(⋅;θ)v(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta)v(⋅;θ) that is nonlinear in its parameters, such as a neural network, the fit is

θk+1∈arg⁡min⁡θ∑i=1m(v(si;θ)−yi)2,yi=(Lvk)(si),\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k+1} \in \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \sum_{i=1}^m \big(v(s_i;\boldsymbol{\theta}) - y_i\big)^2, \qquad y_i = (\Bellman v_k)(s_i),θk+1​∈argθmin​i=1∑m​(v(si​;θ)−yi​)2,yi​=(Lvk​)(si​),
(3)

solved by gradient descent. Its first-order condition is again an orthogonality condition, with test functions that move with the parameters:

∑i=1m(v(si;θ)−yi)∂v(si;θ)∂θj=0for all j.\sum_{i=1}^m \big(v(s_i;\boldsymbol{\theta}) - y_i\big) \frac{\partial v(s_i;\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta_j} = 0 \quad \text{for all } j.i=1∑m​(v(si​;θ)−yi​)∂θj​∂v(si​;θ)​=0for all j.
(4)

The derivatives ∂v/∂θj\partial v/\partial\theta_j∂v/∂θj​ span the tangent space of the model at the current parameters. For a linear model they are the basis functions, and the condition is the sampled Galerkin condition. The targets yiy_iyi​ are held fixed during the fit, so the gradient differentiates only v(si;θ)v(s_i;\boldsymbol\theta)v(si​;θ) and never the operator. This is the semi-gradient of temporal difference learning. The least-squares criterion of Step 3: Impose nnn Conditions on the Residual, Bellman residual minimization, would instead minimize ∑i(v(si;θ)−(Lv(⋅;θ))(si))2\sum_i \big(v(s_i;\boldsymbol\theta) - (\Bellman v(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta))(s_i)\big)^2∑i​(v(si​;θ)−(Lv(⋅;θ))(si​))2 with the same parameters on both sides. Its test functions, ∂v/∂θj−∂(Lv)/∂θj\partial v/\partial\theta_j - \partial(\Bellman v)/\partial\theta_j∂v/∂θj​−∂(Lv)/∂θj​, form the full gradient, and computing them requires differentiating through the max, by the envelope theorem (Theorem 1), or through the log-sum-exp of the smooth Bellman operator. The two criteria have different solutions. Every algorithm in the chapters ahead, from NFQ to NFQCA, fits to fixed targets, and the next chapter studies what happens when the fit is warm-started and stopped after a few gradient steps instead of run to convergence.

Error Bounds When Every Fit Is Accurate¶

Every fit is only approximately right. The averagers of the previous chapter keep the iteration a contraction, but a tree ensemble whose splits follow the targets, or a neural network, is not an averager. This section bounds how far from v∗v^*v∗ fitted value iteration ends with any fit, and how good the returned policy is, assuming only that each fit is accurate.

The finite-horizon chapter answered this for backward recursion with interpolation: with nonnegative weights, the error of the stored values is at most the sum of the interpolation errors of the later stages (Proposition 1). Over an infinite horizon the sum becomes a geometric series.

Let v0v_0v0​ be bounded and let the sequence vkv_kvk​ satisfy ∥vk+1−Lvk∥∞≤ε\|v_{k+1} - \Bellman v_k\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon∥vk+1​−Lvk​∥∞​≤ε for every kkk. Then

∥vk−v∗∥∞≤γk∥v0−v∗∥∞+ε1−γ.\|v_k - v^*\|_\infty \leq \gamma^k \|v_0 - v^*\|_\infty + \frac{\varepsilon}{1-\gamma}.∥vk​−v∗∥∞​≤γk∥v0​−v∗∥∞​+1−γε​.
(5)

Since v∗=Lv∗v^* = \Bellman v^*v∗=Lv∗ and L\BellmanL is a γ\gammaγ-contraction,

∥vk+1−v∗∥∞≤∥vk+1−Lvk∥∞+∥Lvk−Lv∗∥∞≤ε+γ∥vk−v∗∥∞.\|v_{k+1} - v^*\|_\infty \leq \|v_{k+1} - \Bellman v_k\|_\infty + \|\Bellman v_k - \Bellman v^*\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon + \gamma \|v_k - v^*\|_\infty.∥vk+1​−v∗∥∞​≤∥vk+1​−Lvk​∥∞​+∥Lvk​−Lv∗∥∞​≤ε+γ∥vk​−v∗∥∞​.

The value function is an instrument. What we use is the greedy policy, and its loss is bounded by the error of the value function it is greedy for Singh & Yee (1994).

Combining the two, the greedy policies of fitted value iteration are eventually within 2γε/(1−γ)22\gamma\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)^22γε/(1−γ)2 of optimal. The bound asks nothing of the fit except accuracy: no linearity, no particular basis, no structure at all. This is what licenses a tree ensemble or a neural network in place of a table. It also says where the difficulty lies, in three places that the rest of this chapter and the next ones take up.

  1. The error is measured in the sup norm, at every state. A regression controls an average error over the states where targets were computed, and nothing at the states it never saw. The analysis of fitted value iteration by Munos (2007) and Munos & Szepesvári (2008) replaces the sup norm by weighted norms. The price is a concentrability coefficient, which measures how far the state distributions that policies reach can be from the distribution of the data. It is the theoretical form of the coverage problem of batch and offline reinforcement learning.

  2. The fit must be achievable. The bound needs some θ\thetaθ with v(⋅;θ)v(\cdot;\theta)v(⋅;θ) close to Lvk\Bellman v_kLvk​ for every vkv_kvk​ the algorithm produces. The function class must therefore be nearly closed under the Bellman operator, not merely able to represent v∗v^*v∗.

  3. The error must stay bounded. The theorem assumes one ε\varepsilonε for all iterations. If the fit error grows with vkv_kvk​, the bound says nothing, and the two-state example of the previous chapter shows that this happens.

Example: Checking the Bounds on Duck-Hunting Regulations¶

The bounds can be tested on a problem that a government agency solves every year. Each summer, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service chooses the duck-hunting regulations for the Mississippi and Central Flyways from four packages: a closed season, or a restrictive, moderate or liberal one, which differ in season length and bag limit. Since 1995 the choice for mallards has come from a policy computed by stochastic dynamic programming, a program called adaptive harvest management Johnson et al. (1997). The state is two numbers from the May survey: the breeding population NNN of midcontinent mallards and the number PPP of ponds in Prairie Canada, both in millions. Ponds follow an autoregressive process driven by the weather. The population responds to ponds and to the harvest under four models. They disagree on whether hunting deaths add to natural deaths or replace them, and on how strongly reproduction falls as the population grows, and the Service weights them by how well each has predicted past surveys. The reward is the harvest, devalued in proportion when the population is expected to fall below the goal of 8.5 million birds, and the season must close below 4.75 million. We take these equations and numbers from the Service’s report for the 2012 season U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (2012) and discount future harvests by γ=0.98\gamma = 0.98γ=0.98. The model module lists the few details that the report leaves open.

The Service solves this problem the way the finite-horizon chapter solved the reservoir: on a grid of states, with interpolation between the nodes. We do the same with steps of 0.1 million birds and ponds, 12,231 nodes, and bilinear interpolation. Bilinear interpolation is an averager, so value iteration on the grid converges (Theorem 1), and doubling the step changes the values by less than 0.05. Figure 1 compares the result with the table that the Service published for 2012. The two policies prescribe the same package in 126 of the 150 cells of the table and differ by one package in the others. The published policy reacts more strongly to ponds than ours.

The reference solution lets us check Theorem 1 and Proposition 1 against what actually happens. We run fitted value iteration for 400 iterations with five fits. Three are bilinear interpolation on coarser grids, with steps of 2, 1 and 0.5. The other two are regressors trained, at each iteration, on targets at the same 2,000 states drawn uniformly at random: extra trees, which are averagers, and a network with two hidden layers of 64 units, warm-started from the previous iteration. For each fit we measure ε\varepsilonε, the largest fitting error ∣vk+1(s)−(Lvk)(s)∣|v_{k+1}(s) - (\Bellman v_k)(s)|∣vk+1​(s)−(Lvk​)(s)∣ over the reference grid in the last iterations, and compare both bounds with the value error and the policy loss that we compute against the reference.

Fitted value iteration for 400 iterations with γ = 0.98. The fit error is the largest ∣vk+1−Lvk∣|v_{k+1} - \mathrm{L} v_k|∣vk+1​−Lvk​∣ over the 12,231 states of the reference grid in the last 20 iterations. Value error and policy loss are measured against the reference solution, in millions of birds of discounted harvest; the optimal value ranges from about 30 to 51. Same package is the share of reference states where the greedy policy picks the reference package.

The table supports three observations.

  1. Both bounds hold, and both are loose. The value error is 18 to 118 times smaller than ε/(1−γ)\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)ε/(1−γ), and the policy loss is four to five orders of magnitude below 2γε/(1−γ)22\gamma\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)^22γε/(1−γ)2. The bounds charge every iteration’s error at its worst state and let the errors add up in the same direction for 1/(1−γ)=501/(1-\gamma) = 501/(1−γ)=50 years. Neither happens here.

  2. The policy is much more accurate than the value function. The coarsest grid has 45 nodes and a value error of 2.2 million birds, yet it picks the reference package in 96.5% of the states, and its worst policy loss is 0.10 million birds, about a quarter of a percent of the value. A decision depends on the differences between the values of the packages, and much of the fitting error is shared by all four packages, because their successor states are close.

  3. The regressors do about as well as the coarsest grid. With 2,000 targets per iteration, the trees and the network have fitting errors of 0.76 and 1.47, of the same order as the 0.79 of the 45-node grid. The network’s greedy policy reproduces the reference map (panel (c)): it picks the reference package in 98% of the states and loses at most 0.03. The trees lose more, 0.26 at worst. Their fit is piecewise constant, so it is flat where the value has a slope, and the greedy choice between two packages depends on that slope.

With two state variables the Service’s grid is the right tool, and the regressors bring nothing. They become necessary when the state has many dimensions, or when there is no model at all to compute targets from. This chapter has an example of each: the eight-dimensional stopping problem of Example: A Stopping Problem in Eight Dimensions and the satellite collision warnings of Example: Collision Avoidance Learned from Logged Warnings.

Two Expectations in Every Fitted Update¶

Integrals appear in two places in a fitted Bellman update. The first is inside the operator: the transition expectation ∫v(s′) p(ds′∣s,a)\int v(s')\,p(ds'|s,a)∫v(s′)p(ds′∣s,a) that every target contains. The second is over the states: Galerkin and least-squares conditions integrate the residual against test functions, and a regression averages the fitting error over the states where targets were computed. Collocation has only the first integral, which is one reason it was the simplest case.

Write L~\BellmanQuadL for the Bellman operator with the transition expectation replaced by a numerical rule, deterministic or random, and let fitted value iteration run with it, vk+1=P L~vkv_{k+1} = \Proj\,\BellmanQuad v_kvk+1​=PLvk​. The error after one iteration splits into three pieces by the triangle inequality. With v⋆=Lv⋆v^\star = \Bellman v^\starv⋆=Lv⋆,

∥v⋆−vk+1∥=∥v⋆−PL~vk∥≤∥v⋆−PLv⋆∥⏟best approximation+∥PLv⋆−PLvk∥⏟contraction of the current error+∥PLvk−PL~vk∥⏟integration error.\begin{aligned} \|v^\star - v_{k+1}\| &= \|v^\star - \Proj \BellmanQuad v_k\| \\ &\le \underbrace{\|v^\star - \Proj \Bellman v^\star\|}_{\text{best approximation}} + \underbrace{\|\Proj \Bellman v^\star - \Proj \Bellman v_k\|}_{\text{contraction of the current error}} + \underbrace{\|\Proj \Bellman v_k - \Proj \BellmanQuad v_k\|}_{\text{integration error}} . \end{aligned}∥v⋆−vk+1​∥​=∥v⋆−PLvk​∥≤best approximation∥v⋆−PLv⋆∥​​+contraction of the current error∥PLv⋆−PLvk​∥​​+integration error∥PLvk​−PLvk​∥​​.​
(9)

The first term is the best the basis can do, the second shrinks with the iterations when PL\Proj\BellmanPL is a contraction, and the third is the error of the integration rule, which does not shrink as the iterations proceed. In the language of Theorem 1, the integration error is one more contribution to the per-iteration error ε\varepsilonε, and it is amplified by the same 1/(1−γ)1/(1-\gamma)1/(1−γ). This is why the accuracy of the integration rule should match the accuracy of the basis. A degree-10 Chebyshev basis represents a smooth value function to about 10-8, but with a rectangle rule for the expectation the integration error, of order h2h^2h2, dominates the sum, and the basis is wasted.

For low-dimensional problems with a smooth, explicit transition density, deterministic quadrature is the right tool, and the rule is chosen to match the basis: Gauss–Chebyshev nodes with Chebyshev polynomials, Gauss–Legendre with Legendre, Gauss–Hermite with Hermite polynomials and Gaussian shocks, midpoint or trapezoidal rules with piecewise-constant or piecewise-linear elements. With orthogonal collocation the nodes of the basis double as the nodes of the quadrature, and the expectations of the basis functions at the successors of each node can be precomputed once into a matrix, so that each iteration costs a matrix product and a maximization. The fishery used Gauss–Hermite quadrature over its log-normal shock in this way. The same pairing principle governed continuous-time trajectory optimization, where the cost integral and the dynamics were discretized on the same nodes.

Deterministic quadrature needs three things: a state of low dimension, a density that can be evaluated at the nodes, and a cheap model. The problems this part of the book is heading for have none of them. The state of the eight-dimensional stopping problem later in this section needs N8N^8N8 quadrature nodes for a product rule with NNN nodes per axis. A simulator provides draws of s′s's′ and no density. And a logged transition provides exactly one draw, which cannot be chosen. Monte Carlo integration handles all three.

Estimating Bellman Targets by Monte Carlo¶

Monte Carlo integration approximates an expectation by the average of independent draws. For J=E[f(X)]J = \mathbb{E}[f(X)]J=E[f(X)] with X∼pX \sim pX∼p, draw X(1),…,X(N)∼pX^{(1)}, \ldots, X^{(N)} \sim pX(1),…,X(N)∼p and form

J^N=1N∑n=1Nf(X(n)).\hat{J}_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N f\big(X^{(n)}\big).J^N​=N1​n=1∑N​f(X(n)).
(10)

Two properties of this estimator carry the whole chapter. It is unbiased, E[J^N]=J\mathbb{E}[\hat{J}_N] = JE[J^N​]=J, by linearity of expectation. And its variance is σ2/N\sigma^2/Nσ2/N with σ2=Var[f(X)]\sigma^2 = \mathrm{Var}[f(X)]σ2=Var[f(X)], by independence of the draws, so by the central limit theorem

N (J^N−J)⟹N(0,σ2),\sqrt{N}\,(\hat{J}_N - J) \Longrightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),N​(J^N​−J)⟹N(0,σ2),
(11)

and the error decays as N−1/2N^{-1/2}N−1/2. The rate is slow next to high-order quadrature in one dimension, and it is the same in every dimension: Monte Carlo pays in variance, never in an exponential number of nodes. It is also a quadrature rule, with random nodes and equal weights 1/N1/N1/N. Importance sampling changes the distribution of the nodes and compensates with unequal weights, and the view of Monte Carlo as randomized quadrature covers it too.

The cell below checks both properties on a Gaussian with mean 2 and standard deviation 3, with 4,000 repetitions for each sample size. Before looking at the figure, predict what multiplying NNN by four does to the root mean squared error.

The Sampled Bellman Operator¶

For a fixed value function vvv and a state-action pair (s,a)(s,a)(s,a), the transition part of the Bellman operator is the expectation E[v(S′)∣S=s,A=a]\mathbb{E}[v(S') \mid S = s, A = a]E[v(S′)∣S=s,A=a]. If next states S′(1),…,S′(N)S'^{(1)}, \ldots, S'^{(N)}S′(1),…,S′(N) can be drawn from p(⋅∣s,a)p(\cdot \mid s,a)p(⋅∣s,a), by calling a simulator or by acting in the real system, the sample average estimates it. When the reward is random as well, the draws are pairs (r(n),S′(n))(r^{(n)}, S'^{(n)})(r(n),S′(n)), and the one-step return is estimated by

G^N(s,a)=1N∑n=1N[r(n)+γ v(S′(n))],\widehat{G}_N(s,a) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N \Big[r^{(n)} + \gamma\, v\big(S'^{(n)}\big)\Big],GN​(s,a)=N1​n=1∑N​[r(n)+γv(S′(n))],
(12)

which is unbiased for E[r+γv(S′)∣s,a]\mathbb{E}[r + \gamma v(S') \mid s, a]E[r+γv(S′)∣s,a] as long as vvv is fixed. Substituting it into the operator gives the Monte Carlo Bellman operator

(L^Nv)(s)=max⁡a∈AsG^N(s,a).(\widehat{\Bellman}_N v)(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \widehat{G}_N(s,a).(LN​v)(s)=a∈As​max​GN​(s,a).
(13)

Nothing about approximation or projection has entered yet. For a fixed vvv, Monte Carlo provides unbiased, noisy evaluations of (Lv)(s)(\Bellman v)(s)(Lv)(s) at any state, from draws alone. The maximum over the noisy estimates, however, is not unbiased, and the last section of the chapter is about that.

Choosing the States at Which Targets Are Computed¶

The second expectation, over the states, is estimated the same way. Galerkin and least-squares conditions have the form ∫R(s;θ) pi(s) ξ(ds)=0\int R(s;\theta)\, p_i(s)\, \xi(ds) = 0∫R(s;θ)pi​(s)ξ(ds)=0 for a distribution ξ\xiξ over states, and the weighted norm of the residual is ∫R(s;θ)2 ξ(ds)\int R(s;\theta)^2\,\xi(ds)∫R(s;θ)2ξ(ds). The weight www of the previous chapters could be any positive function; for sampling it must be a probability distribution that can be drawn from, which is ξ\xiξ after normalization, or any other distribution with importance weights w/ξw/\xiw/ξ. If states S(1),…,S(M)S^{(1)}, \ldots, S^{(M)}S(1),…,S(M) are drawn from ξ\xiξ, each condition becomes a sample average,

∫R(s;θ) pi(s) ξ(ds)≈1M∑m=1MR(S(m);θ) pi(S(m)),\int R(s;\theta)\, p_i(s)\, \xi(ds) \approx \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^M R\big(S^{(m)};\theta\big)\, p_i\big(S^{(m)}\big),∫R(s;θ)pi​(s)ξ(ds)≈M1​m=1∑M​R(S(m);θ)pi​(S(m)),
(14)

and the least-squares objective becomes the empirical risk 1M∑mR(S(m);θ)2\frac{1}{M}\sum_m R(S^{(m)};\theta)^2M1​∑m​R(S(m);θ)2. This is the regression of Fitted Value Iteration with an Arbitrary Regressor: targets at sampled states, and a fit that minimizes the average error over them. In reinforcement learning ξ\xiξ is rarely chosen; it is the distribution of the states that the data happen to contain, which the previous chapter showed to matter for convergence and the batch experiments of Fitted Q-Iteration on a Fixed Batch of Transitions show to matter for coverage.

With both expectations sampled, the fitted update is

vk+1=PM L^N vk,v_{k+1} = \Proj_M\, \widehat{\Bellman}_N\, v_k,vk+1​=PM​LN​vk​,
(15)

a fit at MMM sampled states of targets that each average NNN sampled successors. It needs no transition density and no state distribution in closed form, only the ability to draw from them. In the typical reinforcement-learning setting N=1N = 1N=1: each recorded transition (si,ai,ri,si′)(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)(si​,ai​,ri​,si′​) supplies one successor, and the target ri+γv(si′)r_i + \gamma v(s'_i)ri​+γv(si′​) has the full variance of a single draw. The variance is then reduced by the fit, which pools information across neighboring states, and by the number of transitions rather than by averaging at a fixed (s,a)(s,a)(s,a). The section after next returns to this choice.

Example: A Stopping Problem in Eight Dimensions¶

The fishery of the earlier chapters has one state variable, and a grid of a few thousand nodes solves it exactly enough to serve as a reference. To see why the choice of fit matters, consider a state with DDD coordinates. An agent watches an index s∈[0,1]Ds \in [0,1]^Ds∈[0,1]D, for instance the prices of DDD assets. Stopping pays the average of the coordinates, sˉ=1D∑ℓsℓ\bar{s} = \frac{1}{D}\sum_\ell s_\ellsˉ=D1​∑ℓ​sℓ​, and ends the problem. Continuing pays nothing, and each coordinate then moves toward a fresh uniform draw, sℓ′=ρsℓ+(1−ρ)ξℓs'_\ell = \rho s_\ell + (1-\rho)\xi_\ellsℓ′​=ρsℓ​+(1−ρ)ξℓ​ with ξℓ∼U[0,1]\xi_\ell \sim U[0,1]ξℓ​∼U[0,1] independent and ρ=0.7\rho = 0.7ρ=0.7. The Bellman equation is

v∗(s)=max⁡{sˉ,  γ E[v∗(ρs+(1−ρ)ξ)]},γ=0.9.v^*(s) = \max\Big\{ \bar{s},\; \gamma\, \mathbb{E}\big[v^*(\rho s + (1-\rho)\xi)\big] \Big\}, \qquad \gamma = 0.9.v∗(s)=max{sˉ,γE[v∗(ρs+(1−ρ)ξ)]},γ=0.9.
(16)

The average sˉ\bar ssˉ is itself a Markov chain, sˉ′=ρsˉ+(1−ρ)ξˉ\bar{s}' = \rho\bar{s} + (1-\rho)\bar{\xi}sˉ′=ρsˉ+(1−ρ)ξˉ​, so v∗v^*v∗ depends on sss only through sˉ\bar ssˉ and can be computed exactly by one-dimensional value iteration. The algorithm does not know this. A grid with 11 nodes per axis has 11D11^D11D nodes: 121 for D=2D = 2D=2, 14,641 for D=4D = 4D=4, and 2.1×1082.1 \times 10^82.1×108 for D=8D = 8D=8, each needing an expectation over a DDD-dimensional successor at every iteration. Fitted value iteration instead computes targets at 2,000 states drawn uniformly from the cube, whatever DDD is, and fits them with an ensemble of extremely randomized trees Ernst et al. (2005) or with a neural network of two hidden layers. All three methods approximate the expectation by the average over the same 32 draws of ξ\xiξ, so they solve the same sample-average problem; the sampled Bellman operator above is this approximation. The errors are measured against the exact v∗v^*v∗ at 5,000 fresh states.

The grid is the most accurate method while it fits in memory, and it is out of reach at D=8D = 8D=8. The trees and the network use the same 2,000 states in every dimension. The average error of the trees roughly doubles each time DDD doubles, while that of the network stays near 0.01; the figure shows that the network has found the one direction along which the value changes. Both have maximum errors several times their average, at the corners of the cube, where few of the sampled states lie. That gap is a first glimpse of the issue that dominates the analysis below and the batch methods of Fitted Q-Iteration on a Fixed Batch of Transitions: a fit is controlled where there are data, and only there.

Action Values: Acting Without a Model¶

The greedy policy of a value function vvv is

π(s)=arg⁡max⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+γ∫v(s′) p(ds′∣s,a)},\pi(s) = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \Big\{ r(s,a) + \gamma \int v(s')\,p(ds'|s,a) \Big\},π(s)=arga∈As​max​{r(s,a)+γ∫v(s′)p(ds′∣s,a)},
(17)

one transition expectation per action at every decision. With a model and a quadrature rule this is a computation; with a simulator it is a Monte Carlo estimate per action, repeated each time the state is visited; with a log it is impossible, because no new successors can be drawn at decision time. The expectation can instead be computed once, during training, and stored. The action-value function of vvv,

q(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∫v(s′) p(ds′∣s,a),q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \int v(s')\,p(ds'|s,a),q(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∫v(s′)p(ds′∣s,a),
(18)

caches the backup of every action, and the greedy policy becomes π(s)=arg⁡max⁡aq(s,a)\pi(s) = \arg\max_{a} q(s,a)π(s)=argmaxa​q(s,a), a maximization over stored values with no integral and no model. The optimal action-value function q⋆q^\starq⋆ satisfies its own Bellman equation, obtained by substituting v⋆(s′)=max⁡a′q⋆(s′,a′)v^\star(s') = \max_{a'} q^\star(s',a')v⋆(s′)=maxa′​q⋆(s′,a′):

q⋆(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∫p(ds′∣s,a) max⁡a′∈As′q⋆(s′,a′).q^\star(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \int p(ds'|s,a)\, \max_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_{s'}} q^\star(s',a').q⋆(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∫p(ds′∣s,a)a′∈As′​max​q⋆(s′,a′).
(19)

The right-hand side defines the Bellman operator on action-value functions, (Lq)(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ E[max⁡a′q(s′,a′)∣s,a](\Bellman q)(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[\max_{a'} q(s',a') \mid s,a](Lq)(s,a)=r(s,a)+γE[maxa′​q(s′,a′)∣s,a], and it is a γ\gammaγ-contraction in the sup norm by the same argument as for vvv: the maximum over a′a'a′ does not increase sup-norm distances, and the expectation does not either. Everything in the previous chapter transfers. Fitted value iteration on qqq is fitted Q-iteration, its error bounds hold with (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) in place of sss, averagers remain safe, and the function class now takes the action as an input or has one output per action. What changes is the cost accounting: the expectations are evaluated during the iterations, at the state-action pairs where targets are computed, and acting afterwards is cheap.

Algorithm 2 (Fitted Q-Iteration with a Model)

Input Given an MDP (S,A,P,R,γ)(S, A, P, R, \gamma)(S,A,P,R,γ), base points B⊂S\mathcal{B} \subset SB⊂S, function approximator class q(s,a;θ)q(s,a; \boldsymbol{\theta})q(s,a;θ), maximum iterations NNN, tolerance ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, initial parameters θ0\boldsymbol{\theta}_0θ0​

  1. Initialize θ0\boldsymbol{\theta}_0θ0​ (e.g., random initialization)

  2. n←0n \leftarrow 0n←0

  3. repeat

    1. D←∅\mathcal{D} \leftarrow \emptysetD←∅

    2. For each (s,a)∈B×A(s,a) \in \mathcal{B} \times A(s,a)∈B×A:

      1. ys,a←r(s,a)+γ∫p(ds′∣s,a)max⁡a′∈Aq(s′,a′;θn)y_{s,a} \leftarrow r(s,a) + \gamma \int p(ds'|s,a)\max_{a' \in A} q(s',a'; \boldsymbol{\theta}_n)ys,a​←r(s,a)+γ∫p(ds′∣s,a)maxa′∈A​q(s′,a′;θn​)

    4. δ←1∣D∣∣A∣∑(s,a)∈D×A(q(s,a;θn+1)−q(s,a;θn))2\delta \leftarrow \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}||A|}\sum_{(s,a) \in \mathcal{D} \times A} (q(s,a; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{n+1}) - q(s,a; \boldsymbol{\theta}_n))^2δ←∣D∣∣A∣1​∑(s,a)∈D×A​(q(s,a;θn+1​)−q(s,a;θn​))2

The expectation in the target can be computed by quadrature when the model allows it, or estimated by NNN draws of the successor from p(⋅∣s,a)p(\cdot|s,a)p(⋅∣s,a), averaging max⁡a′q(si′,a′)\max_{a'} q(s'_i, a')maxa′​q(si′​,a′) over them. The fitting step is the one of Fitted Value Iteration with an Arbitrary Regressor, with its initialization θinit\boldsymbol\theta_{\text{init}}θinit​ and its optimization budget KKK written out because the next chapter varies both.

One Sampled Successor per Target¶

Most reinforcement learning algorithms do not draw NNN successors per state-action pair. They work with a data set of transition tuples D={(si,ai,ri,si′)}i=1M\mathcal{D} = \{(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)\}_{i=1}^MD={(si​,ai​,ri​,si′​)}i=1M​, each recording the one successor that was observed when aia_iai​ was executed in sis_isi​, and the target of a tuple is yi=ri+γmax⁡a′q(si′,a′)y_i = r_i + \gamma \max_{a'} q(s'_i, a')yi​=ri​+γmaxa′​q(si′​,a′), with N=1N = 1N=1.

This design has two origins. In some settings it is a constraint. A robot that executes an action observes one outcome and cannot rewind to the same state to sample another; the same holds for a clinical trial, a manufacturing process, or any interaction that costs something. Many settings in which reinforcement learning is applied have no such constraint. Game emulators save and restore states, physics simulators reset to any configuration, and software environments are cloned for free. The second origin is historical. Reinforcement learning grew out of models of animal learning, in which an organism experiences one consequence per action and learns from a stream of experience, and temporal-difference learning, Q-learning and the actor-critic methods were designed for that stream.

The convention persisted where the constraint did not, and it shaped the algorithms. They store and manipulate tuples rather than state-action pairs with several successors. They reduce variance through the function approximator, which pools targets from nearby states, and through the number of transitions, rather than by averaging at a fixed (s,a)(s,a)(s,a). And they treat the two expectations asymmetrically: the outer one, over states, is sampled with whatever budget is convenient, a whole data set, a replay buffer of a million transitions, or one transition per step, while the inner one is sampled once. In a domain with a cheap, resettable simulator and high-variance targets, averaging several successors per (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) is a direct variance reduction that current practice rarely uses.

Temporal-Difference Learning: One Transition per Update¶

The sampled fitted update above draws a batch of transitions, computes targets, and fits. Temporal-difference learning takes the opposite extreme, one transition at a time, with a gradient step in place of the fit. For policy evaluation with linear features v(s;θ)=ϕ(s)⊤θv(s;\theta) = \boldsymbol\phi(s)^\top\thetav(s;θ)=ϕ(s)⊤θ, its target is the Galerkin system (20) of the previous chapter, Aθ=b\mathbf{A}\theta = \mathbf{b}Aθ=b with A=Φ⊤Ξ(I−γPπ)Φ\mathbf{A} = \boldsymbol\Phi^\top\boldsymbol\Xi(\mathbf{I} - \gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi)\boldsymbol\PhiA=Φ⊤Ξ(I−γPπ​)Φ and b=Φ⊤Ξ rπ\mathbf{b} = \boldsymbol\Phi^\top\boldsymbol\Xi\,\mathbf{r}_\pib=Φ⊤Ξrπ​, whose solution is the fixed point of the projected Bellman equation v=PLπvv = \Proj\BellmanPi vv=PLπ​v. Both A\mathbf{A}A and b\mathbf{b}b are expectations over a state drawn from ξ\xiξ and a successor drawn from Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​, the two expectations of Two Expectations in Every Fitted Update, so each transition gives an unbiased estimate of them.

TD(0) draws a state sss from ξ\xiξ, a successor s′s's′ from Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ and the reward rrr, and moves the parameters along the temporal difference,

θ←θ+α ϕ(s)(r+γϕ(s′)⊤θ−ϕ(s)⊤θ).\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha\, \boldsymbol\phi(s)\big(r + \gamma\boldsymbol\phi(s')^\top\theta - \boldsymbol\phi(s)^\top\theta\big).θ←θ+αϕ(s)(r+γϕ(s′)⊤θ−ϕ(s)⊤θ).
(20)

The expected increment is α(b−Aθ)\alpha(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\theta)α(b−Aθ), the residual of (20). The theory of stochastic approximation Kushner & Yin (2003) says that, with step sizes that decrease suitably, the iterates follow the ordinary differential equation θ˙=b−Aθ\dot\theta = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\thetaθ˙=b−Aθ, which converges to the solution of (20) from every start if and only if every eigenvalue of A\mathbf{A}A has a positive real part. Fitted policy evaluation in the same coordinates is θk+1=θk+(Φ⊤ΞΦ)−1(b−Aθk)\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k + (\boldsymbol\Phi^\top\boldsymbol\Xi\boldsymbol\Phi)^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\theta_k)θk+1​=θk​+(Φ⊤ΞΦ)−1(b−Aθk​), one step of the same expected update with the step size replaced by the inverse of the mass matrix. The two algorithms share their fixed point and their matrix, and differ in how they step toward it. LSTD (Solving the Galerkin System Directly: LSTD) does not step at all: it estimates A\mathbf{A}A and b\mathbf{b}b from the transitions and solves the system.

Proposition 2 of the previous chapter showed that on-policy, with ξ\xiξ the stationary distribution of Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​, A\mathbf{A}A is positive definite. Its eigenvalues then have positive real parts, and TD(0) converges to the solution of the projected Bellman equation Tsitsiklis & Van Roy (1997). The same inequality makes fitted evaluation a contraction and the LSTD system uniquely solvable: on-policy, the three solvers are stable for the same reason.

The analysis extends to TD(λ\lambdaλ), which bootstraps from a geometric mixture of multi-step returns. Its fixed point solves v=PLπ(λ)vv = \Proj\BellmanPi^{(\lambda)}vv=PLπ(λ)​v with the multi-step operator Lπ(λ)=(1−λ)∑k≥0λkLπk+1\BellmanPi^{(\lambda)} = (1-\lambda)\sum_{k \geq 0}\lambda^k\BellmanPi^{k+1}Lπ(λ)​=(1−λ)∑k≥0​λkLπk+1​, which is a contraction in ∥⋅∥ξ\|\cdot\|_\xi∥⋅∥ξ​ with modulus αλ=γ(1−λ)/(1−γλ)\alpha_\lambda = \gamma(1-\lambda)/(1-\gamma\lambda)αλ​=γ(1−λ)/(1−γλ), and the fixed point satisfies ∥vλ−vπ∥ξ≤(1−αλ2)−1/2∥Pvπ−vπ∥ξ\|v_\lambda - v_\pi\|_\xi \leq (1 - \alpha_\lambda^2)^{-1/2}\|\Proj v_\pi - v_\pi\|_\xi∥vλ​−vπ​∥ξ​≤(1−αλ2​)−1/2∥Pvπ​−vπ​∥ξ​ Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis (1996)Bertsekas (2011). At λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1 the modulus is zero, the targets are Monte Carlo returns, and the fixed point is the best approximation Pvπ\Proj v_\piPvπ​; at λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0 the constant is the (1−γ2)−1/2(1-\gamma^2)^{-1/2}(1−γ2)−1/2 of the previous chapter. Bertsekas and Yu developed this projected-equation view into a general method for large linear systems, with error bounds that are sharper than the contraction argument because they use the data to estimate how P\ProjP and Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ interact Bertsekas & Yu (2009)Yu & Bertsekas (2010)Bertsekas (2011).

The two conditions, A\mathbf{A}A with eigenvalues in the right half plane for TD and a spectral radius of γPPπ\gamma\Proj\mathbf{P}_\piγPPπ​ below one for fitted evaluation, are different conditions on the same matrices. In the two-state counterexample of the previous chapter they coincide. There is one feature, so A\mathbf{A}A is the scalar ξ1(1−2γ)+4ξ2(1−γ)\xi_1(1 - 2\gamma) + 4\xi_2(1-\gamma)ξ1​(1−2γ)+4ξ2​(1−γ), and the fitted iteration multiplies θ\thetaθ by 1−A/(ξ1+4ξ2)1 - \mathbf{A}/(\xi_1 + 4\xi_2)1−A/(ξ1​+4ξ2​), which is the factor 6γ/56\gamma/56γ/5 of the previous chapter when ξ1=ξ2=1/2\xi_1 = \xi_2 = 1/2ξ1​=ξ2​=1/2. Both fail when A<0\mathbf{A} < 0A<0. With uniform weights that happens for γ>5/6\gamma > 5/6γ>5/6, and with the stationary weighting ξ=(0,1)\xi = (0, 1)ξ=(0,1) it never happens. The code below runs sampled TD(0) on the example with γ=0.9\gamma = 0.9γ=0.9 and three weightings.

Off-Policy Evaluation and Its Repairs¶

When the states are weighted by a distribution ξ\xiξ that is not stationary for Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​, which is the situation of learning about one policy from the data of another, the Jensen step of the on-policy argument fails, and with it Proposition 2. The previous chapter noted that the fixed point itself can then be far from vπv_\pivπ​ Kolter (2011). The solver can fail as well: TD(0) can diverge even when the projected equation is perfectly well posed.

The classical example is Baird’s star Baird (1995), in the form given by Sutton & Barto (2018). There are seven states and eight weights: state i≤6i \leq 6i≤6 has value 2θi+θ82\theta_i + \theta_82θi​+θ8​, and state 7 has value θ7+2θ8\theta_7 + 2\theta_8θ7​+2θ8​. The target policy moves every state to state 7, the behavior policy moves to a uniformly chosen state, all rewards are zero, and γ=0.99\gamma = 0.99γ=0.99. The features span all of R7\mathbb{R}^7R7, so P\ProjP is the identity, PLπ=Lπ\Proj\BellmanPi = \BellmanPiPLπ​=Lπ​ is a contraction, and fitted policy evaluation converges in any norm. The difficulty lies entirely in the solver. The cell below iterates the expected updates of three methods from Sutton and Barto’s starting point, with the states weighted uniformly as the behavior policy visits them, and reports the largest ∣v(s;θ)∣|v(s;\theta)|∣v(s;θ)∣ along the way; the true value is zero.

Under the uniform weighting, γPπ\gamma\mathbf{P}_\piγPπ​ has ξ\xiξ-norm about 2.6, so it is not a contraction in that norm, and the TD matrix has an eigenvalue with negative real part. Expected TD(0) diverges, and its values reach the thousands after 2000 updates although every quantity in the problem is bounded. This is the first leg of the deadly triad, with no maximum and no neural network: linear features, bootstrapping, and off-policy weighting suffice.

Three families of repairs keep the projected equation and change the solver or the weighting.

  1. Importance sampling reweights each update by the ratio of the target and behavior probabilities of the action taken Precup et al. (2001). This makes the expected update use the target policy’s transitions, but not the target policy’s state distribution, so the matrix A\mathbf{A}A above, which already uses Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​, is unchanged; ratios over whole trajectories correct the distribution too, at the price of a variance that can grow exponentially with the horizon.

  2. Gradient TD methods minimize the mean squared projected Bellman error ∥P(Lπvθ−vθ)∥ξ2\|\Proj(\BellmanPi v_\theta - v_\theta)\|_\xi^2∥P(Lπ​vθ​−vθ​)∥ξ2​, which is zero exactly when the Galerkin conditions hold, by true stochastic gradient descent with a second set of weights that estimates P(Lπvθ−vθ)\Proj(\BellmanPi v_\theta - v_\theta)P(Lπ​vθ​−vθ​) Sutton et al. (2009). The objective has the TD fixed point as its minimizer for any weighting, and gradient descent on it is stable. In the cell, TDC, the variant called TD with gradient correction in that paper, brings the values down from 12 to about 2 within 500 updates and then stalls there: its stability is bought with slow progress, a common observation with these methods.

  3. Emphatic TD reweights the update at each state by a follow-on trace, which on average replaces ξ\xiξ in A\mathbf{A}A by the emphasis f=(I−γPπ⊤)−1ξf = (\mathbf{I} - \gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi^\top)^{-1}\xif=(I−γPπ⊤​)−1ξ Sutton et al. (2016). The resulting matrix Φ⊤F(I−γPπ)Φ\boldsymbol\Phi^\top\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{I} - \gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi)\boldsymbol\PhiΦ⊤F(I−γPπ​)Φ with F=diag(f)\mathbf{F} = \text{diag}(f)F=diag(f) is positive definite for any behavior when the features are independent, by an argument close to that of Proposition 2, and the method converges Yu (2015). Baird’s features are not independent, and the matrix is only semidefinite, which the zero printed in the cell reflects. In the cell, its values go to zero. The fixed point is the solution of a projected equation with the emphasis weighting, not with ξ\xiξ, so it is a different approximation of vπv_\pivπ​.

LSTD avoids the stability question altogether, because it solves Aθ=b\mathbf{A}\theta = \mathbf{b}Aθ=b directly. Off-policy, it computes the same fixed point as TD, with the same possible loss of accuracy, whenever A\mathbf{A}A is invertible Bertsekas & Yu (2009).

The Deadly Triad, and What Is Known with the Maximum¶

Sutton & Barto (2018) call the combination of function approximation, bootstrapping (targets built from the current estimate) and off-policy data the deadly triad: any two are manageable, all three can diverge. Baird’s star has all three, without a maximum. Q-learning adds the maximum, and with it a target policy that changes with the parameters. What is known for sampled updates with the maximum follows the two routes of the previous chapter.

On the sup-norm route, the averager argument survives sampling. Q-learning with soft state aggregation Singh et al. (1995) and Q-learning on action values interpolated from a finite set of states Szepesvári & Smart (2004) converge, under the same sign condition on the weights as in the deterministic case.

On the weighted route, the results are special cases or weaker conclusions.

  • Q-learning with linear features converges when the behavior policy is close enough to the greedy policy of every parameter it visits, a condition on feature covariances that Melo et al. (2008) make precise. It holds near on-policy learning and fails in general off-policy.

  • SARSA(0), which evaluates the policy it follows and improves it at every step, cannot diverge with linear features: its weights stay in a bounded region, inside which they may chatter without converging Gordon (2000).

  • Approximate policy iteration with SARSA evaluation converges to a unique solution when the improvement step produces soft policies that are Lipschitz functions of the action values, with a small enough constant Perkins & Precup (2002). A softmax with a high enough temperature satisfies this condition and the greedy policy does not.

  • Gradient methods for control, such as Greedy-GQ, minimize the projected Bellman error of the greedy policy by stochastic gradient and converge to a stationary point of that objective, not necessarily to a solution of the projected equation Maei et al. (2010).

  • Optimistic exploration with a Gibbs policy guarantees that a solution of the projected equation for Q-learning exists and that the iterates stay bounded; convergence remains open Meyn (2023).

Error bounds for fitted iterations on sampled data add a statistical error to the bounds of Error Bounds When Every Fit Is Accurate, as in the finite-sample analysis of fitted value iteration by Munos & Szepesvári (2008). They need the function class to be closed, or nearly closed, under the Bellman operator, a condition called Bellman completeness Chen & Jiang (2019). The design choices that keep neural fitted Q-iteration stable in practice, target networks among them, are the subject of the next chapter.

  1. One feature, one condition. In the two-state counterexample of the previous chapter, show that fitted evaluation converges if and only if expected TD(0) is stable. Then construct a two-feature example in which one is stable and the other is not. Hint: the fitted iteration is a preconditioned TD step of size one.

  2. How far off-policy? In Baird’s star, compute the eigenvalues of A\mathbf{A}A as a function of γ\gammaγ and find the discount below which none has a negative real part. Then mix the uniform weighting with the stationary distribution of the target policy, ξβ=(1−β) uniform+β e7\xi_\beta = (1-\beta)\,\text{uniform} + \beta\,\mathbf{e}_7ξβ​=(1−β)uniform+βe7​, and find the smallest β\betaβ for which none has a negative real part at γ=0.99\gamma = 0.99γ=0.99.

Maximization Bias in Sampled Targets¶

Each estimate G^N(s,a)\widehat{G}_N(s,a)GN​(s,a) is unbiased, and the maximum over them is not. Fix a state sss and a value function vvv, and write the true continuation value and its estimate as

μ(s,a)=∫v(s′) p(ds′∣s,a),μ^N(s,a)=1N∑i=1Nv(si′),si′∼p(⋅∣s,a),\mu(s,a) = \int v(s')\,p(ds' \mid s,a), \qquad \hat{\mu}_N(s,a) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N v(s'_i), \quad s'_i \sim p(\cdot|s,a),μ(s,a)=∫v(s′)p(ds′∣s,a),μ^​N​(s,a)=N1​i=1∑N​v(si′​),si′​∼p(⋅∣s,a),
(21)

so that (L^Nv)(s)=max⁡a{r(s,a)+γμ^N(s,a)}(\widehat{\Bellman}_N v)(s) = \max_a \{r(s,a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}_N(s,a)\}(LN​v)(s)=maxa​{r(s,a)+γμ^​N​(s,a)}. Let a⋆a^\stara⋆ be the action that maximizes the true backup. The maximum of a collection is at least as large as any of its members, so

E[max⁡a{r(s,a)+γμ^N(s,a)}]≥E[r(s,a⋆)+γμ^N(s,a⋆)]=r(s,a⋆)+γμ(s,a⋆)=(Lv)(s).\mathbb{E}\big[\max_a \{r(s,a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}_N(s,a)\}\big] \ge \mathbb{E}\big[r(s,a^\star) + \gamma \hat{\mu}_N(s,a^\star)\big] = r(s,a^\star) + \gamma \mu(s,a^\star) = (\Bellman v)(s).E[amax​{r(s,a)+γμ^​N​(s,a)}]≥E[r(s,a⋆)+γμ^​N​(s,a⋆)]=r(s,a⋆)+γμ(s,a⋆)=(Lv)(s).
(22)

The inequality is strict whenever more than one action has a nonzero variance: the maximization picks whichever action received a positive noise, and that inflated estimate becomes the target. This is Jensen’s inequality for the maximum, E[max⁡aYa]≥max⁡aE[Ya]\mathbb{E}[\max_a Y_a] \ge \max_a \mathbb{E}[Y_a]E[maxa​Ya​]≥maxa​E[Ya​], since the maximum is convex. The same inequality is the reason that deterministic policies are optimal in MDPs (Theorem 2), where it says that randomizing over actions cannot beat the best one; here it says that maximizing over noisy estimates cannot be unbiased.

The bias does not average out with more draws of the same estimate, and it compounds. Monte Carlo value iteration vk+1=L^Nvkv_{k+1} = \widehat{\Bellman}_N v_kvk+1​=LN​vk​ builds its targets at iteration k+1k+1k+1 from a vkv_kvk​ that is already biased upward, so E[vk]≥E[vk−1]≥⋯≥v⋆\mathbb{E}[v_k] \ge \mathbb{E}[v_{k-1}] \ge \cdots \ge v^\starE[vk​]≥E[vk−1​]≥⋯≥v⋆, and the inflated values feed back into the next maximization. The cell below holds every true action value at zero, draws five noisy samples per action, and measures the bias of the maximum as the number of actions grows, next to the estimator of the next subsection.

Double Estimators: Separating Selection from Evaluation¶

The bias comes from using one noisy estimate for two jobs. Decompose the estimate into its mean and its noise, μ^N(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa\hat{\mu}_N(s,a) = \mu(s,a) + \varepsilon_aμ^​N​(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa​ with E[εa]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_a] = 0E[εa​]=0. The standard target is

Y=r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)+γεa^,a^=arg⁡max⁡a{r(s,a)+γμ(s,a)+γεa},Y = r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \mu(s,\hat a) + \gamma \varepsilon_{\hat a}, \qquad \hat a = \arg\max_a \{r(s,a) + \gamma \mu(s,a) + \gamma \varepsilon_a\},Y=r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)+γεa^​,a^=argamax​{r(s,a)+γμ(s,a)+γεa​},
(23)

and the same εa^\varepsilon_{\hat a}εa^​ that made a^\hat aa^ win is added to its value. Double Q-learning Van Hasselt et al. (2016) breaks this coupling with two independent estimates of every action, μ^N(1)(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa(1)\hat{\mu}^{(1)}_N(s,a) = \mu(s,a) + \varepsilon^{(1)}_aμ^​N(1)​(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa(1)​ and μ^N(2)(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa(2)\hat{\mu}^{(2)}_N(s,a) = \mu(s,a) + \varepsilon^{(2)}_aμ^​N(2)​(s,a)=μ(s,a)+εa(2)​, with ε(1)\varepsilon^{(1)}ε(1) and ε(2)\varepsilon^{(2)}ε(2) independent. The first selects and the second evaluates:

a^=arg⁡max⁡a{r(s,a)+γμ^N(1)(s,a)},Y=r(s,a^)+γμ^N(2)(s,a^).\hat a = \arg\max_{a} \big\{r(s,a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}^{(1)}_N(s,a)\big\}, \qquad Y = r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}^{(2)}_N(s,\hat a).a^=argamax​{r(s,a)+γμ^​N(1)​(s,a)},Y=r(s,a^)+γμ^​N(2)​(s,a^).
(24)

The selected action a^\hat aa^ is random, a function of ε(1)\varepsilon^{(1)}ε(1) alone. Conditioning on it,

E[Y]=Eε(1)[Eε(2)[r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)+γεa^(2)∣a^]]=Eε(1)[r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)],\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon^{(1)}}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon^{(2)}}\big[r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \mu(s,\hat a) + \gamma \varepsilon^{(2)}_{\hat a} \mid \hat a\big]\Big] = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon^{(1)}}\big[r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \mu(s,\hat a)\big],E[Y]=Eε(1)​[Eε(2)​[r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)+γεa^(2)​∣a^]]=Eε(1)​[r(s,a^)+γμ(s,a^)],
(25)

because ε(2)\varepsilon^{(2)}ε(2) is independent of a^\hat aa^, so that E[εa^(2)∣a^]=E[εa^(2)]=0\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\hat a} \mid \hat a] = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\hat a}] = 0E[εa^(2)​∣a^]=E[εa^(2)​]=0. The evaluation noise contributes nothing on average. What remains is the selection bias: a^\hat aa^ is more often an action whose ε(1)\varepsilon^{(1)}ε(1) was positive than one whose true value is highest, so E[μ(s,a^)]≤max⁡aμ(s,a)\mathbb{E}[\mu(s,\hat a)] \le \max_a \mu(s,a)E[μ(s,a^)]≤maxa​μ(s,a), and the double estimator is biased downward. In Figure 4 the maximum estimator grows more optimistic as the number of actions grows, while the double estimator has no bias: every action has the same true value there, so selecting the wrong one costs nothing and the selection bias is zero. When the true values differ, the double estimator is biased downward instead, by much less than the maximum is biased upward. Removing the evaluation bias, the reuse of the winning noise, removes most of the overestimation.

Remark 1 (Two Q-functions instead of two sets of draws)

The argument assumes two independent sets of draws from p(⋅∣s,a)p(\cdot|s,a)p(⋅∣s,a) for every state-action pair, which a log never provides and a simulator provides only by resetting. The practical implementation keeps two Q-functions instead, trained on different data or updated at different times, for instance an online network and a slowly updated copy of it. Their errors are then less correlated than the errors of a single network used twice, which gives part of the independence that the argument needs. This is Double DQN, in the next chapter (Double DQN).

The algorithm below writes the principle out with Monte Carlo targets. Two Q-functions alternate roles: at line 9 the first selects the action and at line 12 the second evaluates it, and lines 10 and 13 do the same with the roles exchanged. The mechanism is the same whether the Q-functions are tables or fitted functions, and with single-sample data (N=1N = 1N=1) the two Q-functions are trained on different subsets or at different frequencies to approximate the independence.

  3. repeat

Other Corrections¶

Three other approaches keep a single estimate and correct the maximum itself. They differ in how much they assume about the noise.

The correction can be learned. Keane & Wolpin (1994) treated the bias δ(s)=E[(L^Nv)(s)]−(Lv)(s)≥0\delta(s) = \mathbb{E}[(\widehat{\Bellman}_N v)(s)] - (\Bellman v)(s) \ge 0δ(s)=E[(LN​v)(s)]−(Lv)(s)≥0 as a quantity to estimate and subtract. It cannot be computed directly, but it depends on observable features of the state: the number of actions, the sample size, and the spread of the action values, since the bias is large when several actions are close and small when one dominates. At a small set of states, they ran both a high-fidelity evaluation of the backup, with many draws, and the NNN-draw estimate used by the iteration, and regressed the gap on those features; during value iteration the predicted bias is subtracted from the raw maximum. The template, simulate on a subset and interpolate everywhere, is common in econometric dynamic programming. It has seen little use in reinforcement learning, because the high-fidelity evaluations are expensive and a misspecified regression feeds its own error back into the values.

The correction can be derived, under a distributional assumption. Lee et al. (2013)Lee & Powell (2019) assumed Gaussian noise of standard deviation σ\sigmaσ on the estimates of MMM actions, in which case the expected maximum of the noises follows from extreme value theory,

E[max⁡aεa]≈σ(CEbM+bM),bM=2log⁡M−log⁡log⁡M−log⁡4π,\mathbb{E}\Big[\max_{a} \varepsilon_a\Big] \approx \sigma \left(\frac{C_{\mathrm{E}}}{b_M} + b_M\right), \qquad b_M = \sqrt{2\log M - \log\log M - \log 4\pi},E[amax​εa​]≈σ(bM​CE​​+bM​),bM​=2logM−loglogM−log4π​,
(26)

with CE≈0.5772C_{\mathrm{E}} \approx 0.5772CE​≈0.5772 the Euler–Mascheroni constant, and the target is corrected by subtracting this amount with σ\sigmaσ estimated from repeated rewards at the same (s,a)(s,a)(s,a). The formula is exact for a single-state problem whose only noise is in the rewards, and it is a first-order correction otherwise; with heavier tails than Gaussian it undercorrects. It replaces the regression of the learned correction by a closed form, at the price of the Gaussian assumption.

The maximum can be replaced. D'Eramo et al. (2016) weight each action by the probability that it is the best one under a Gaussian model of the estimates, wa=P(a∈arg⁡max⁡a′μ^a′)w_a = \mathbb{P}\big(a \in \arg\max_{a'} \hat{\mu}_{a'}\big)wa​=P(a∈argmaxa′​μ^​a′​), and use ∑awaμ^a\sum_a w_a \hat{\mu}_a∑a​wa​μ^​a​ in place of max⁡aμ^a\max_a \hat{\mu}_amaxa​μ^​a​. The weighted estimator sits between the optimism of the maximum and the pessimism of the double estimator, and adapts to the gaps between actions: when one action dominates its weight is near one and the estimator is the maximum, and when several are close their estimates are averaged. It needs a variance estimate per action and one integral per action, which limits it to small action sets. The smooth Bellman operator of the regularized chapter also replaces the hard maximum by an average, with weights set by a temperature rather than by estimated uncertainty. A last option changes neither the target nor the operator but the loss of the fit, so that overestimates are penalized more than underestimates; the next chapter takes it up with Gumbel regression.

Fitted Q-Iteration on a Fixed Batch of Transitions¶

The Bellman operator on action values contains an expectation under the transition law, which we write PPP over transitions τ=(s,a,r,s′)\tau = (s, a, r, s')τ=(s,a,r,s′):

(Lq)(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∫max⁡a′q(s′,a′) P(ds′∣s,a).(\Bellman q)(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \int \max_{a'} q(s',a')\, P(ds' \mid s,a).(Lq)(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ∫a′max​q(s′,a′)P(ds′∣s,a).
(27)

A batch algorithm never sees PPP. It receives a data set D={(si,ai,ri,si′)}i=1N\mathcal{D} = \{(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)\}_{i=1}^ND={(si​,ai​,ri​,si′​)}i=1N​ and works with the empirical distribution

P^D=1N∑τ∈Dδτ,\hat{P}_{\mathcal{D}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{D}} \delta_\tau,P^D​=N1​τ∈D∑​δτ​,
(28)

where δτ\delta_\tauδτ​ is a point mass at the transition τ\tauτ. Sampling from P^D\hat{P}_{\mathcal{D}}P^D​ means picking a recorded transition uniformly at random, and the expectation of any function of a transition under PPP is estimated by its average over the data set, the sample-average estimator of this chapter applied to transitions. Fitted Q-iteration on a batch is value iteration under this empirical law. The target of a transition is yi=ri+γmax⁡a′q(si′,a′)y_i = r_i + \gamma \max_{a'} q(s'_i, a')yi​=ri​+γmaxa′​q(si′​,a′), with the one successor that was recorded, and the fit averages the error of the targets over the transitions in the data set. In the language of statistics this is a plug-in estimate: where the algorithm needs the unknown PPP, it substitutes P^D\hat{P}_{\mathcal{D}}P^D​.

Remark 2 (The empirical distribution as a probability measure)

The empirical distribution P^D=1N∑τ∈Dδτ\hat{P}_{\mathcal{D}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{D}} \delta_{\tau}P^D​=N1​∑τ∈D​δτ​ is a discrete probability measure over NNN points, whether the state and action spaces are continuous or discrete. For any measurable set A⊆S×A×R×SA \subseteq \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} \times \mathbb{R} \times \mathcal{S}A⊆S×A×R×S,

P^D(A)=1N∑τ∈D1[τ∈A]=∣{τ∈D:τ∈A}∣N,\hat{P}_{\mathcal{D}}(A) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{D}} \mathbb{1}[\tau \in A] = \frac{|\{\tau \in \mathcal{D} : \tau \in A\}|}{N},P^D​(A)=N1​τ∈D∑​1[τ∈A]=N∣{τ∈D:τ∈A}∣​,
(29)

so it assigns probability 1/N1/N1/N to each recorded tuple and zero elsewhere. A transition that never occurred has no weight, which is the formal statement of the coverage problem that the two experiments below exhibit.

Algorithm 4 (Fitted Q-Iteration on a Batch)

Input: Dataset D={(si,ai,ri,si′)}i=1N\mathcal{D} = \{(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)\}_{i=1}^ND={(si​,ai​,ri​,si′​)}i=1N​, function approximator q(s,a;θ)q(s,a; \boldsymbol{\theta})q(s,a;θ), discount factor γ\gammaγ, maximum iterations nmax⁡n_{\max}nmax​

Output: Learned Q-function parameters θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ

  1. Initialize θ0\boldsymbol{\theta}_0θ0​

  2. n←0n \leftarrow 0n←0

  3. repeat \quad // Outer loop: value iteration

  4. \quad // Construct the regression data set with Bellman targets

  5. \quad X(n)←{(si,ai):(si,ai,ri,si′)∈D}X^{(n)} \leftarrow \{(s_i, a_i) : (s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i) \in \mathcal{D}\}X(n)←{(si​,ai​):(si​,ai​,ri​,si′​)∈D}

  6. \quad for each (si,ai,ri,si′)∈D(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i) \in \mathcal{D}(si​,ai​,ri​,si′​)∈D do

  7. \quad\quad yi(n)←ri+γmax⁡a′∈Aq(si′,a′;θn)y_i^{(n)} \leftarrow r_i + \gamma \max_{a' \in \mathcal{A}} q(s'_i, a'; \boldsymbol{\theta}_n)yi(n)​←ri​+γmaxa′∈A​q(si′​,a′;θn​)

  8. \quad end for

  9. \quad // Inner loop: fit the Q-function to the targets

  10. \quad θn+1←fit(X(n),y(n),θinit,K)\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n+1} \leftarrow \texttt{fit}(X^{(n)}, y^{(n)}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{init}}, K)θn+1​←fit(X(n),y(n),θinit​,K)

  11. \quad n←n+1n \leftarrow n+1n←n+1

  12. until convergence or n≥nmax⁡n \geq n_{\max}n≥nmax​

  13. return θn\boldsymbol{\theta}_nθn​

The state-action pairs X(n)X^{(n)}X(n) are the same at every iteration; only the targets change, because they are computed with the current Q-function. The fit operation in line 10 minimizes ∑iℓ(q(si,ai;θ),yi(n))\sum_i \ell(q(s_i, a_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}), y_i^{(n)})∑i​ℓ(q(si​,ai​;θ),yi(n)​) for a loss ℓ\ellℓ, by whatever procedure the function class calls for, from an initialization θinit\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{init}}θinit​ and with an optimization budget KKK. Supervised learning would initialize at random and run to convergence. The two original batch algorithms differ in exactly these choices.

Ernst et al. (2005) instantiated the template with extremely randomized trees, an ensemble whose prediction is the average of the targets in a leaf. Each fit grows the trees from scratch, a cold start, and runs to completion, since tree construction has no incremental form. A tree with a fixed partition is an averager, so the convergence theorem of the previous chapter applies once the partitions stop changing, and trees take high-dimensional inputs without feature design. Riedmiller (2005) replaced the ensemble by a neural network q(s,a;θ)q(s,a;\boldsymbol\theta)q(s,a;θ), which interpolates smoothly across the state-action space, and fitted it by gradient descent (RProp, chosen for its insensitivity to hyperparameters) until the loss stopped decreasing. The network is warm-started: each fit begins from the parameters of the previous iteration, which is natural for a gradient method and is the first of the choices that the next chapter turns into DQN.

Remark 3 (Goal states in neural fitted Q-iteration)

For episodic tasks with goal states S+S^+S+ and forbidden states S−S^-S−, Riedmiller modified the targets:

yi(n)={c(si,ai,si′)if si′∈S+ (goal reached)C−if si′∈S− (forbidden state, typically C−=1)c(si,ai,si′)+γmax⁡a′q(si′,a′;θn)otherwise,y_i^{(n)} = \begin{cases} c(s_i, a_i, s'_i) & \text{if } s'_i \in S^+ \text{ (goal reached)} \\ C^- & \text{if } s'_i \in S^- \text{ (forbidden state, typically } C^- = 1\text{)} \\ c(s_i, a_i, s'_i) + \gamma \max_{a'} q(s'_i, a'; \boldsymbol{\theta}_n) & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}yi(n)​=⎩⎨⎧​c(si​,ai​,si′​)C−c(si​,ai​,si′​)+γmaxa′​q(si′​,a′;θn​)​if si′​∈S+ (goal reached)if si′​∈S− (forbidden state, typically C−=1)otherwise,​
(30)

where c(s,a,s′)c(s, a, s')c(s,a,s′) is the immediate cost. A goal state has no future cost and no bootstrapped term, a forbidden state carries a fixed penalty, and every other state uses the Bellman backup. The hint-to-goal heuristic adds synthetic transitions from goal states with target zero, which pins the Q-function to zero in the goal region and encodes the boundary condition explicitly.

Experiment: Scheduling from Logged Transitions¶

The reduced inference-scheduling MDP in Infinite-Horizon MDPs has an exact value-iteration solution because its transition matrix is known. Suppose instead that only a fixed table of transitions is retained. Each row contains a reduced state (p,d)(p,d)(p,d), a scheduling action, the cost ccc, and the next reduced state. The generic reward-maximizing form above becomes a cost-minimizing form after a sign change. FQI can reuse those rows, but it receives no direct evidence for a state-action region that the behavior policy never visits. Any prediction there comes from the regressor’s inductive bias.

Each transition row is sampled from the finite MDP, not logged directly from vLLM. Its arrival model comes from the normalized Azure trace, while its phase rates and powers come from one NVIDIA L4 measurement run of Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct served by vLLM 0.28.0. The data sets therefore inherit a measured hardware calibration and all of the reduced model’s aggregation assumptions.

Two sampling procedures produce matched data sets of 50,000 transitions. The broad data set draws a reduced state uniformly and then draws uniformly among its feasible actions. The narrow data set follows trajectories from the empty system under a decode-priority heuristic and selects a random feasible action with probability 0.05. Both use seed 0 and the same MDP. Their different state-action sampling distributions are the controlled change.

Each fitted-Q sweep constructs targets

yi(n)=ci+0.99min⁡u′∈A(si′)qn(si′,u′)y_i^{(n)}=c_i+0.99\min_{u'\in\mathcal A(s_i')} q_n(s_i',u')yi(n)​=ci​+0.99u′∈A(si′​)min​qn​(si′​,u′)
(31)

and fits a joint state-action Extra-Trees regressor. The ensemble contains 200 trees with maximum depth 12 and minimum leaf size 2. The random seed is 0; successive tree fits use the deterministic seeds 0 through 49 across 50 fitted-Q sweeps. The three scheduling actions enter as a one-hot input, matching the joint state-action representation in the generic batch algorithm above. Before each fit, rows with the same state and action are merged into one point whose target is their average and whose weight is their count. The minimum leaf size of 1 therefore counts distinct state-action pairs, not rows: a larger value would force every leaf to average the targets of at least two different pairs, which blurs the small differences between actions in the same state.

Changing only the sampling distribution tests how coverage affects an otherwise identical FQI procedure. The exact dynamic-programming policy and both fitted policies are evaluated on the same 2,000 seeded episodes, each 300 steps long. Return and policy disagreement measure agreement with the reduced MDP objective and its exact solution. Mean waiting time, dropped arrivals, and observed state-action coverage locate operational differences. Decode stalls count periods in which decode jobs were active but the policy did something else. In this model they are not errors: the exact policy stalls decode on purpose while it prefills to grow the batch.

Exact dynamic programming and the two fitted-Q policies use the same 2,000 seeded episodes of 300 steps. Coverage is computed from the feasible state-action pairs present in each fixed transition buffer.

import pandas as pd

fqi_metrics = pd.read_csv(
    "artifacts/inference_serving/metrics_fqi.csv"
).set_index("controller")
fqi_metrics[
    [
        "mean_discounted_return",
        "mean_queue_length",
        "mean_waiting_time_s",
        "mean_decode_stalls",
        "mean_dropped_arrivals",
        "coverage_fraction",
        "policy_disagreement_fraction",
    ]
].T.rename_axis("metric").round(3)
Loading...

Download every fitted-Q metric (CSV)

The broad buffer covers every feasible state-action pair, and its fitted policy disagrees with the exact policy in 6 of the 49 states (12.24 percent). All six lie next to the switching curve, where the exact policy prefills and the fitted policy decodes. Each of these state-action pairs appears about 340 times in the buffer, so the errors do not come from missing data. In those states the exact action values of prefill and decode differ by at most 1.24, while the values themselves range from 254 to 891. A regressor that is accurate to a fraction of a percent can still rank two actions this close in the wrong order. The broad policy’s mean discounted return is -242.25, compared with -230.04 for the exact policy, and its mean waiting time is 5.76 seconds rather than 5.24.

The narrow buffer covers 41.73 percent of feasible pairs and disagrees with the exact policy in 19 states (38.78 percent). In 15 of those states the buffer contains no visit to the action that the fitted policy selects. The log follows decode priority, which never prefills while a request is decoding, so the regressor has no data on the batching decisions that the exact policy makes. Its choices there are extrapolations: it idles in several states with six requests decoding, and it prefills past the point where the exact policy decodes. Its mean discounted return is -286.08, its mean waiting time is 11.20 seconds, and it drops 1.40 arrivals per episode against 0.20 for the exact policy. Return is the negative of discounted cost, so higher values are better.

The two data sets have equal size, so the difference between their policies cannot be attributed to the number of transition rows. The broad buffer’s errors come from approximation where the action gap is small; the narrow buffer’s errors come from coverage, where the behavior policy never took the action in question. These are the first and the third difficulty named after the error bound of Error Bounds When Every Fit Is Accurate: a fit is accurate on average, not at the states where two actions are nearly tied, and it is controlled only where there are data.

The hardware calibration is measured, while training and evaluation remain inside the stated 49-state MDP. These results concern offline coverage under that abstraction. They are not a benchmark of vLLM scheduling or of NVIDIA L4 hardware across deployments.

def fit_fqi(
    mdp: SchedulingMDP,
    dataset: TransitionDataset | None = None,
    *,
    behavior: Literal["uniform", "decode_priority"] = "uniform",
    number_transitions: int = 50_000,
    sweeps: int = 50,
    number_trees: int = 200,
    maximum_depth: int = 12,
    minimum_leaf_size: int = 1,
    exploration_probability: float = 0.05,
    random_seed: int = 0,
    reference_policy: np.ndarray | None = None,
) -> FQISolution:
    """Fit a joint state-action Extra-Trees approximation of the cost-to-go."""

    mdp.validate()
    if sweeps <= 0 or number_trees <= 0:
        raise ValueError("sweeps and number_trees must be positive")
    samples = dataset or generate_transition_dataset(
        mdp,
        behavior=behavior,
        number_transitions=number_transitions,
        exploration_probability=exploration_probability,
        random_seed=random_seed,
    )
    sample_features = _features(mdp, samples.state, samples.action)
    pair_id = samples.state * 3 + samples.action
    unique_pair, inverse = np.unique(pair_id, return_inverse=True)
    unique_states = unique_pair // 3
    unique_actions = unique_pair % 3
    unique_features = _features(mdp, unique_states, unique_actions)
    counts = np.bincount(inverse).astype(float)
    model: ExtraTreesRegressor | None = None
    target = samples.cost.copy()

    all_states = np.repeat(np.arange(mdp.states.shape[0]), 3)
    all_actions = np.tile(np.arange(3), mdp.states.shape[0])
    all_features = _features(mdp, all_states, all_actions)
    for sweep in range(sweeps):
        aggregated_target = np.bincount(inverse, weights=target) / counts
        model = ExtraTreesRegressor(
            n_estimators=number_trees,
            max_depth=maximum_depth,
            min_samples_leaf=minimum_leaf_size,
            random_state=random_seed + sweep,
            n_jobs=1,
        )
        model.fit(unique_features, aggregated_target, sample_weight=counts)
        predicted = model.predict(all_features).reshape(mdp.states.shape[0], 3)
        predicted = np.where(mdp.valid_actions, predicted, np.inf)
        next_minimum = np.min(predicted[samples.next_state], axis=1)
        target = samples.cost + mdp.gamma * next_minimum
    assert model is not None
    q_values = model.predict(all_features).reshape(mdp.states.shape[0], 3)
    q_values = np.where(mdp.valid_actions, q_values, np.inf)
    policy = np.argmin(q_values, axis=1).astype(int)
    labels = tuple(SCHEDULING_ACTIONS[int(action)] for action in policy)
    disagreement = None
    if reference_policy is not None:
        reference = np.asarray(reference_policy, dtype=int)
        if reference.shape != policy.shape:
            raise ValueError("reference_policy has an incompatible shape")
        disagreement = float(np.mean(policy != reference))
    return FQISolution(
        model=model,
        q_values=q_values,
        policy=policy,
        policy_labels=labels,
        dataset=samples,
        sweeps=sweeps,
        random_seed=random_seed,
        policy_disagreement_fraction=disagreement,
    )

Example: Collision Avoidance Learned from Logged Warnings¶

This example has no model, only a log. When a satellite and another object, most often a piece of debris, are predicted to pass close to each other, the operator receives about three conjunction data messages per day over the week before the time of closest approach. Each message gives a collision probability estimated from the latest tracking. The operator can plan an avoidance maneuver or wait for the next message. Waiting buys information, because most alarms go away as the tracking improves. It also makes the maneuver more expensive: closer to the encounter, a larger change of velocity is needed for the same miss distance, and there is less time to plan. ESA plans its maneuvers at least two days before closest approach, and its missions in low orbit react to collision probabilities between 10-5 and 10-4 Uriot et al. (2022). ESA released the messages of 13,154 conjunctions of its satellites for a machine-learning competition Uriot et al. (2022), and we use them as the log.

We pose an optimal stopping problem on these sequences. A decision is taken at each message received at least two days before closest approach, and once more at the two-day deadline with the latest message. A maneuver ttt days before closest approach costs c(t)=(1+2/t)/2c(t) = (1 + 2/t)/2c(t)=(1+2/t)/2, in units of a maneuver two days out. An event without a maneuver costs C=105C = 10^5C=105 times the collision probability of its last message, the best estimate available, so that a maneuver at the deadline breaks even at a probability of 10-5. The state is what the operator knows at a decision: the time ttt to closest approach, the latest log-probability ρ\rhoρ, and the age of that message. The costs are teaching choices, and ESA’s analysts look at much more than one number.

Two features of the problem let fitted Q-iteration work from the log alone. A maneuver ends the problem at a known cost, so q(s,maneuver)=c(t)q(s, \text{maneuver}) = c(t)q(s,maneuver)=c(t) needs no learning. And waiting does not change which messages arrive: the released sequences contain no maneuvers, so each one shows what follows “wait”. Fitted Q-iteration only has to learn W(s)=q(s,wait)W(s) = q(s, \text{wait})W(s)=q(s,wait), by regression on the logged transitions (si,si′)(s_i, s_i')(si​,si′​) with targets

yi={C pfinalif si is the deadline,min⁡{c(ti′), Wk(si′)}otherwise,Wk+1=fit⁡({(si,yi)}).y_i = \begin{cases} C\, p_{\text{final}} & \text{if } s_i \text{ is the deadline,} \\ \min\{c(t_i'),\, W_k(s_i')\} & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \qquad W_{k+1} = \operatorname{fit}\big(\{(s_i, y_i)\}\big).yi​={Cpfinal​min{c(ti′​),Wk​(si′​)}​if si​ is the deadline,otherwise,​Wk+1​=fit({(si​,yi​)}).
(32)

The minimum over the two actions is the max⁡\maxmax of the Bellman operator for costs. There is no expectation to compute: each logged successor is one draw of s′s's′, the one-successor targets of Action Values: Acting Without a Model. We fit extra trees, the averager of tree-based FQI Ernst et al. (2005), on the logged decision epochs, and judge every policy out of sample: each event is decided by a policy fitted without it.

PolicyManeuversManeuver costExpected collision costTotalMissed

Totals over the 11,942 conjunctions with a message at least 2 days before closest approach, in units of a maneuver two days out. The expected collision cost of an event without a maneuver is 1e+05 times the collision probability of its last message. Missed counts the events whose last message exceeds the break-even probability of 10-5 and that received no maneuver. The fitted Q-iteration rows are out of sample: each event is decided by a policy fitted without it (5-fold cross-validation by event), averaged over three random splits.

Maneuvering at the first alarm is safe but wasteful: it makes 742 maneuvers for 62 events that needed one, because 92 of every 100 alarms resolve (Figure 7, panel (a)). Waiting until the deadline and then acting on the latest message halves the cost. This rule is what an operator would write by hand. Fitted Q-iteration was told neither that waiting pays nor at what probability to act, and it comes within about 7% of the hand rule, 313 against 291. Its learned rule (panel (c)) waits through a new alarm more than three days out unless the probability is twenty to forty-five times the break-even value, in which case it maneuvers early, while a maneuver is still cheap. The bar comes down as the deadline nears, but at the deadline it still asks for about three times the break-even probability, a bet that later messages will come down, and that bet misses more of the events that needed a maneuver, 20 against 6 for the hand rule. Two choices decide whether fitted Q-iteration works here at all, and both follow from the error analysis of the previous chapters.

  1. The fit must fit the right thing. The raw target C pfinalC\, p_{\text{final}}Cpfinal​ is heavy-tailed. One event in the log ends at a probability of 2% and costs about 2,070 if nothing is done, more than three times the cost of all other events together. Extra trees predict the average of the targets in a leaf, so this one cost is shared by every state in the leaves where its epochs fall, and those states look dangerous. Fitted on all events, the raw-target policy makes 342 maneuvers; fitted without that single event, 141. Out of sample it makes 374 maneuvers and costs 441, half again as much as the hand rule. The second version fits the ratio yi/(C 10ρi)y_i / (C\, 10^{\rho_i})yi​/(C10ρi​), the cost relative to what the current message alone predicts, and multiplies the fit back. The regressor then learns a correction factor to the operator’s own estimate. For the dangerous event this factor stays between 0.7 and 7, an ordinary value, and the policy makes 166 maneuvers with the event in the data and 175 without it.

  2. The fit is only as good as the data where decisions are made. Five in six of the 123,882 decision epochs have probabilities below 10-7, where waiting is plainly right, and we leave them out of the fit. Only 62 events needed a maneuver. This is the coverage problem behind the concentrability coefficients of Error Bounds When Every Fit Is Accurate: the regression error that matters is the one at the few states where the two actions are close, and no amount of data elsewhere reduces it. The hindsight policy, at 147, is not a target: it knows the estimate of the messages that arrive after the deadline, which no policy can use.
