What Remains: Online Data and Continuous Actions¶

Fitted Q-iteration on a fixed log, as this chapter leaves it, still differs from NFQCA in two ways.

First, its data are fixed, and each fit runs to completion before the targets change. Online reinforcement learning works from a buffer that changes as the agent acts, and a neural fit is warm-started and stopped after a few gradient steps. The next chapter merges the fit with the outer loop, which produces the target network and the replay buffer of DQN.

Second, it maximizes over a finite set of actions. Every target contains max⁡a′q(s′,a′;θ)\max_{a'} q(s',a';\theta)maxa′​q(s′,a′;θ). When the action is continuous, a torque or a dose, that maximum is a nonlinear program, to be solved once for every target at every iteration. NFQCA Hafner & Riedmiller (2011) trains a second network, an actor πw(s)≈arg⁡max⁡aq(s,a;θ)\pi_{\boldsymbol w}(s) \approx \arg\max_a q(s,a;\theta)πw​(s)≈argmaxa​q(s,a;θ), and uses it in the target in place of the maximum. The critic qqq is fitted by regression against fixed targets, exactly as in this chapter, and the actor by gradient ascent on the critic. In the terms of Approximate Policy Iteration, NFQCA is approximate policy iteration with one fitted evaluation sweep per improvement, that is, a fitted version of modified policy iteration (Algorithm 4) in which the improvement step is learned as well. The amortized action optimization chapter develops it, together with its online descendants DDPG and TD3. The smooth Bellman operator meets the same obstacle in the partition function over a continuous action set (Continuous Action and State Spaces), and soft actor-critic resolves it in the same way.

What fitted value iteration assumedWhat replaces itWhere
State values v(s)v(s)v(s)Action values q(s,a)q(s,a)q(s,a), so acting needs no modelAction Values: Acting Without a Model
Exact expectation in the targetOne sampled successor per transitionAction Values: Acting Without a Model
Targets at chosen statesA fixed batch of logged transitions (FQI, NFQ)Fitted Q-Iteration on a Fixed Batch of Transitions
A fixed batch, each fit run to completionA replay buffer and a target network (DQN)Deep Q-networks
Maximum over a finite action setA learned actor in the target (NFQCA, DDPG, TD3)Amortized action optimization

Exercises¶

The exercises follow the chapter: the fitted iteration, its regressor and its error bounds, single estimators and their effect inside the iteration, then logged data. Exercise 6 reuses the code of the eight-dimensional stopping problem, Exercise 12 is a short simulation and Exercise 18 is a short program.

Exercise 1 (Fitting the backup or minimizing the residual)

Return to the two-state counterexample: v(1;θ)=θv(1;\theta) = \thetav(1;θ)=θ, v(2;θ)=2θv(2;\theta) = 2\thetav(2;θ)=2θ, every reward zero, state 1 moves to state 2 and state 2 stays put.

  1. Bellman residual minimization chooses θ\thetaθ to minimize ∑s(v(s;θ)−(Lv(⋅;θ))(s))2\sum_s \big(v(s;\theta) - (\Bellman v(\cdot;\theta))(s)\big)^2∑s​(v(s;θ)−(Lv(⋅;θ))(s))2 with equal weights. Write this objective and show that its minimizer is θ=0\theta = 0θ=0 for every γ\gammaγ.

  2. Gradient descent on that objective uses the full gradient. Show that it converges for every γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1 with a small enough step, while fitted value iteration diverges for γ>5/6\gamma > 5/6γ>5/6.

  3. Why is Bellman residual minimization rarely used despite this? Consider what an unbiased estimate of (v(s;θ)−E[r+γv(s′;θ)])2\big(v(s;\theta) - \mathbb{E}[r + \gamma v(s';\theta)]\big)^2(v(s;θ)−E[r+γv(s′;θ)])2 requires when the successor is random, and connect it to the one-successor targets of Action Values: Acting Without a Model.

Solution to Exercise 1

  1. The objective is (θ−2γθ)2+(2θ−2γθ)2=θ2[(1−2γ)2+4(1−γ)2](\theta - 2\gamma\theta)^2 + (2\theta - 2\gamma\theta)^2 = \theta^2\big[(1-2\gamma)^2 + 4(1-\gamma)^2\big](θ−2γθ)2+(2θ−2γθ)2=θ2[(1−2γ)2+4(1−γ)2], a parabola whose coefficient is positive for γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1. Its minimizer is θ=0\theta = 0θ=0.

  2. Gradient descent on a positive-definite quadratic converges for any step size below 2/c2/c2/c, where ccc is its curvature. Fitted value iteration does not descend this objective: it holds the target fixed and fits it, which is the semi-gradient, and the semi-gradient map θ↦65γθ\theta \mapsto \tfrac65\gamma\thetaθ↦56​γθ has modulus 65γ>1\tfrac65\gamma > 156​γ>1 for γ>5/6\gamma > 5/6γ>5/6, so it is not a contraction.

  3. Squaring the residual of a single sampled successor gives E[(v(s)−r−γv(s′))2]\mathbb{E}\big[(v(s) - r - \gamma v(s'))^2\big]E[(v(s)−r−γv(s′))2], which equals the squared residual plus the variance of r+γv(s′)r + \gamma v(s')r+γv(s′). The minimizer is biased toward functions with small variance of the successor value. An unbiased estimate needs two independent successors of the same state, the double-sampling problem, which a log with one successor per transition cannot provide.

Exercise 2 (Accurate fits, bad iteration)

In the two-state counterexample, the function class contains v∗v^*v∗ exactly. Why does fitted value iteration still diverge, and why does Theorem 1 not prevent it?

Solution to Exercise 2

The least-squares fit is not an averager: it maps the constant target to a line that overshoots at state 2. Its sup-norm operator norm is 6/56/56/5, so the modulus 6γ/56\gamma/56γ/5 of the composition exceeds one when γ>5/6\gamma > 5/6γ>5/6. The fit error at iteration kkk is proportional to θk\theta_kθk​, so there is no single ε\varepsilonε that bounds it for all kkk, and the theorem’s assumption fails.

Exercise 3 (Reading the bounds)

Fitted value iteration with γ=0.9\gamma = 0.9γ=0.9 starts from v0=0v_0 = 0v0​=0, and ∥v∗∥∞=10\|v^*\|_\infty = 10∥v∗∥∞​=10. Every fit is accurate to ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1 in the sup norm.

  1. Bound ∥v50−v∗∥∞\|v_{50} - v^*\|_\infty∥v50​−v∗∥∞​ with Theorem 1, and separate the part that more iterations remove from the part that they do not.

  2. Bound the loss of the greedy policy of v50v_{50}v50​ with Proposition 1.

  3. The duck-harvest table reports policy losses four to five orders of magnitude below the second bound. Name the two places in the proofs where the worst case is charged, and say why neither happens there.

Solution to Exercise 3

  1. ∥v50−v∗∥∞≤0.950⋅10+0.1/0.1=0.052+1\|v_{50} - v^*\|_\infty \le 0.9^{50} \cdot 10 + 0.1/0.1 = 0.052 + 1∥v50​−v∗∥∞​≤0.950⋅10+0.1/0.1=0.052+1. Further iterations shrink the first term only; the second, ε/(1−γ)=1\varepsilon/(1-\gamma) = 1ε/(1−γ)=1, is the price of the fits and stays.

  2. The greedy loss is at most 2γ1−γ⋅1.052≈18.9\tfrac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma} \cdot 1.052 \approx 18.91−γ2γ​⋅1.052≈18.9, nearly twice ∥v∗∥∞\|v^*\|_\infty∥v∗∥∞​, so the bound says nothing useful here.

  3. The value bound charges every fitting error at its worst state and lets the errors add in the same direction at every iteration. The greedy bound charges the worst value error twice, once for each of the two actions being compared. In the duck problem the fitting errors are much smaller than ε\varepsilonε at most states, they do not align over the 50-year horizon, and much of the error is common to all four packages, so it cancels in the comparison that decides the action.

Exercise 4 (Weighting shift)

If the fitting distribution puts almost no mass on an important region of the state space, what failure should you expect?

Solution to Exercise 4

The fit may be accurate under the weighted norm yet poor in that neglected region, leading to bad values or decisions there. In the error bound of fitted value iteration, this shows up as a large sup-norm error, or, in the weighted analysis, as a large concentrability coefficient.

Exercise 5 (Designing a convergent fitted iteration)

Pick a problem from an earlier chapter that has a continuous state: the reservoir of the finite-horizon chapter, the storm-surge barrier, or the fishery. Design a fitted value iteration for it that is guaranteed to converge, run it, and compare its greedy policy with the exact one. Then replace the fit by a neural network and report what changes: the number of iterations, the stability of the iterates, and the policy loss. Explain the differences with the results of this chapter and the previous one.

Solution to Exercise 5

Any averager gives the guarantee: multilinear interpolation on a grid, state aggregation, or kkk-nearest neighbors on sampled states. A report should state the fit, the states where targets are computed, the tolerance, and the policy loss measured against an exact or fine-grid solution. With the network, expect the iterates to wander by an amount comparable to the fit error rather than converge, as in the duck-harvest experiment, and a policy whose errors concentrate where the data are sparse or two actions are close.

Exercise 6 (An averager on the eight-dimensional problem)

In the code of the eight-dimensional stopping problem, add a fit by kkk-nearest neighbors (sklearn.neighbors.KNeighborsRegressor) with k=1k = 1k=1, 10 and 50, and record the largest change max⁡i∣vk+1(si)−vk(si)∣\max_i |v_{k+1}(s_i) - v_k(s_i)|maxi​∣vk+1​(si​)−vk​(si​)∣ at each iteration.

  1. Check that the changes shrink by at least the factor γ=0.9\gamma = 0.9γ=0.9 per iteration, as Theorem 1 guarantees. Do they for the trees and the network?

  2. Compare the mean and largest errors with those of the trees and the network at D=8D = 8D=8. Which value of kkk is best, and why does a large kkk hurt most at the corners of the cube?

Solution to Exercise 6

The changes shrink geometrically, by a factor of about 0.43 to 0.55 per iteration, faster than γ\gammaγ, because the stopping reward caps the values, and they reach 10-14 within the 40 iterations. With k=10k = 10k=10 at D=8D = 8D=8 the mean error is about 0.022 and the largest about 0.155, between the trees (0.031) and the network (0.013) on average. Larger kkk averages targets over a larger neighborhood; at a corner of the cube all neighbors lie on one side, so the prediction is pulled toward the interior, and the largest error grows to about 0.2 at k=50k = 50k=50. For the trees and the network the measurement is worth making, because no theorem predicts its outcome: the splits of the trees depend on the targets, and the network has no sign or normalization constraint.

Exercise 7 (Sign before simulation)

Several actions have equal true values and independent noisy estimates. What sign do you expect for the bias of their maximum?

Solution to Exercise 7

Positive. Maximization preferentially selects estimates with favorable noise, so the expected maximum exceeds the common true value.

Exercise 8 (Double estimation)

Which dependence is broken when one estimate selects the maximizing action and an independent estimate evaluates it, and which bias remains?

Solution to Exercise 8

The evaluation noise is made independent of the lucky noise that caused the selection, which removes the reuse of the same positive error for both jobs. The selection bias remains: the chosen action is still more often one whose first estimate was lucky, so the double estimator is biased slightly downward.

Exercise 9 (Sample sizes)

A simulator returns successor values with standard deviation σ=3\sigma = 3σ=3.

  1. How many draws give a root mean squared error of 0.01 for one expectation?

  2. A fitted iteration needs one such expectation for each of 2,000 states and 4 actions. How many simulator calls does one iteration cost, and how would the cost change if the state had twice as many coordinates?

  3. By Theorem 1, what does an integration error of 0.01 per iteration contribute to the final value error with γ=0.95\gamma = 0.95γ=0.95?

Solution to Exercise 9

  1. σ/N=0.01\sigma/\sqrt N = 0.01σ/N​=0.01 gives N=(3/0.01)2=90,000N = (3/0.01)^2 = 90{,}000N=(3/0.01)2=90,000.

  2. 2,000×4×90,000=7.2×1082{,}000 \times 4 \times 90{,}000 = 7.2 \times 10^82,000×4×90,000=7.2×108 calls per iteration. The Monte Carlo rate does not depend on the dimension, so the count does not change unless σ\sigmaσ does; a product quadrature rule would need NDN^DND nodes instead.

  3. At most 0.01/(1−0.95)=0.20.01/(1 - 0.95) = 0.20.01/(1−0.95)=0.2, added to the error of the fit.

Exercise 11 (When the double estimator does worse)

Two actions have true values μ1=0\mu_1 = 0μ1​=0 and μ2=−1\mu_2 = -1μ2​=−1, and each estimate has Gaussian noise of standard deviation 1.

  1. For the maximum estimator, use E[max⁡(X1,X2)]=μ1Φ(δ/ϑ)+μ2Φ(−δ/ϑ)+ϑ ϕ(δ/ϑ)\mathbb{E}[\max(X_1, X_2)] = \mu_1\Phi(\delta/\vartheta) + \mu_2\Phi(-\delta/\vartheta) + \vartheta\,\phi(\delta/\vartheta)E[max(X1​,X2​)]=μ1​Φ(δ/ϑ)+μ2​Φ(−δ/ϑ)+ϑϕ(δ/ϑ) with δ=μ1−μ2\delta = \mu_1 - \mu_2δ=μ1​−μ2​ and ϑ=2\vartheta = \sqrt2ϑ=2​, where Φ\PhiΦ and ϕ\phiϕ are the standard Gaussian distribution and density, to compute its bias.

  2. For the double estimator, the selected action is wrong with probability Φ(−δ/ϑ)\Phi(-\delta/\vartheta)Φ(−δ/ϑ). Compute its bias.

  3. Which estimator is closer to the truth here? Relate the answer to the two sources of bias in Maximization Bias in Sampled Targets, and to the case of equal values in Figure 4.

  1. Φ(−1/2)=0.240\Phi(-1/\sqrt2) = 0.240Φ(−1/2​)=0.240 and ϕ(1/2)=0.311\phi(1/\sqrt2) = 0.311ϕ(1/2​)=0.311, so the expected maximum is −0.240+2×0.311=0.200-0.240 + \sqrt2 \times 0.311 = 0.200−0.240+2​×0.311=0.200, a bias of +0.20.

With equal values the selection costs nothing and the double estimator is unbiased; with a gap of the size of the noise, selection bias dominates, and it is negative. Removing evaluation bias does not remove selection bias, which is why the double estimator is pessimistic rather than unbiased in general.

Exercise 14 (Many successors or many transitions)

A resettable simulator can return several successors of the same state and action. With a fixed budget of simulator calls per iteration, compare two uses on the eight-dimensional stopping problem of Example: A Stopping Problem in Eight Dimensions: many states with one successor each, or a quarter as many states with four successors each. Measure the error of the fitted value function and of its greedy policy, and explain the result with the two expectations of Two Expectations in Every Fitted Update: which error does each choice reduce?

Solution to Exercise 14

This exercise is open-ended. More successors per state reduce the variance of each target, which a regression would otherwise have to average out across nearby states. More states reduce the error of the fit itself and extend coverage. Which wins depends on the noise of the targets relative to the smoothness of the value: a problem with very noisy transitions and a smooth value favors more successors, and a problem whose value varies a lot across the state space favors more states.

Exercise 15 (Offline support)

Why is a highly accurate regression fit still dangerous for actions poorly represented in an offline dataset?

Solution to Exercise 15

The fit is unconstrained off the data support. Maximization can select extrapolated action values that are numerically large but unsupported by transitions in the dataset.

Exercise 16 (Matched coverage comparison)

The two inference-scheduling buffers contain the same number of transitions. Why can the buffer with fewer distinct state-action pairs still attain lower training error while producing a worse policy?

Solution to Exercise 16

Repeated transitions make the empirical regression problem easier on the visited region, but they supply no Bellman targets for omitted actions and states. Greedy action selection can therefore depend on unsupported extrapolation even when the in-buffer fit is accurate.

Exercise 17 (Scaling the targets)

In the collision-avoidance example, why did one event with a 2% collision probability change the maneuvers of the fitted policy at hundreds of other states, and what did fitting a ratio instead of the raw cost change?

Solution to Exercise 17

Extra trees predict the average of the targets in a leaf, so a single cost three times larger than all the others combined raises the prediction of every state that shares a leaf with that event’s epochs. Fitting the cost relative to the current message’s own estimate turns the target into a correction factor of ordinary size, so the event no longer dominates the leaves that contain it.

Exercise 18 (Coverage on a chain)

Build a chain of ten states 0,…,90, \ldots, 90,…,9 with two actions. Action “right” moves one state to the right with probability 0.9 and stays with probability 0.1; “left” moves one state to the left in the same way. The reward is 1 on entering or staying in state 9, and γ=0.9\gamma = 0.9γ=0.9.

  1. Log 5,000 transitions from uniformly random states with uniformly random actions, and run fitted Q-iteration with a table as the fit: each target is averaged over the transitions of its state-action pair, and pairs with no data keep the value 0. Evaluate the greedy policy exactly from state 0.

  2. Repeat with a log in which the behavior policy always moves left in states 5 to 8.

  3. Explain why the second policy fails in states 0 to 4, where the log has data for both actions.

Solution to Exercise 18

With the broad log the greedy policy moves right everywhere and its value from state 0 is 3.90, the optimal value. With the narrow log, “right” has no data in states 5 to 8, so its value there stays at 0, which ties with “left” and loses the tie. The policy moves left in states 5 to 8, and the value it attains from state 0 is 0. In states 0 to 4 both actions have data, but the targets of “right” are built from the values of states 1 to 5, which are wrong: the error in the uncovered states propagates backward through the bootstrapped targets. A fit that generalizes, such as trees on the state index, could extrapolate “right” from state 4 or 9, and that extrapolation would decide the result, which is the situation of the narrow inference-scheduling buffer.

Exercise 19 (Where the actor enters)

Which part of fitted Q-iteration does the actor of NFQCA replace, and why is it needed only for continuous actions?

Solution to Exercise 19

It replaces the maximization over next actions inside each Bellman target. With a finite action set the maximum is computed by enumeration; with a continuous action set it is a nonlinear program for every target, and the actor amortizes those programs into one trained network.

Summary and Forward Look¶

Fitted value iteration computes Bellman targets at chosen states and fits a regressor to them. Collocation and Galerkin projection are two fitting rules, and regression with trees or neural networks is the one that scales, as the eight-dimensional stopping problem showed. Fitted Bellman updates contain two expectations, inside the operator and over the states, and either can be estimated from samples. The sample average is unbiased, its error falls as N−1/2N^{-1/2}N−1/2 whatever the dimension, and it adds a per-iteration error that the bound of the previous chapter absorbs. Sampling makes the model optional: a simulator or a log of transitions suffices, which is the setting of reinforcement learning. Acting on a sampled value function would require sampling at decision time, so the action-value function q(s,a)q(s,a)q(s,a) stores the backup of each action instead, and fitted Q-iteration is fitted value iteration on qqq. Temporal-difference learning solves the Galerkin system of the previous chapter one transition at a time; it is stable on-policy for the same reason that the projected equation contracts, and off-policy it can diverge even when the equation is well posed, which importance sampling, gradient TD and emphatic TD repair in different ways. The maximum over noisy estimates is biased upward, and the bias compounds through the iterations; using one estimate to select the action and an independent one to value it removes the larger part of the bias, and learned, analytic or weighted corrections are the alternatives.

Fitted Q-iteration on data is fitted value iteration with the model replaced by the empirical distribution of a buffer: targets from recorded transitions, one successor each, and a fit that averages its error over them. The two experiments located the errors of a fitted policy. In the scheduling log with full coverage, the policy erred only where two actions were nearly tied, an approximation error that more data would not remove; in the log that followed one heuristic, it erred where the heuristic had never tried the exact policy’s action, a coverage error that no regressor can repair. On ESA’s collision warnings, fitted Q-iteration learned from the log alone a rule within about 7% of the one an operator would write by hand, once its targets were scaled so that one rare event could not dominate the fit.

Every fit in this chapter ran to completion on data that did not change. Deep Q-networks lets the data grow as the agent acts and merges the fit with the outer loop, which produces the target network, the replay buffer and DQN.
